transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um, I came in because I’m having a really hard time staying with things mentally, especially at work. I’m a secondary school teacher, so there’s a lot of reading and marking and planning, and I’ll sit down with a stack of essays or a curriculum document fully intending to get through it properly. I’ll have my pen out, laptop open, everything set up, and then maybe ten minutes later I realize I’ve just been staring at the same page.

It’s not that I don’t care about the work — I do — but my mind sort of drifts off into three other things, and I’m not actually taking in what’s in front of me. Then I have to reread the same paragraph or the same student response again and again, and it feels like I’m losing time without noticing it. It’s been frustrating enough that I thought I should actually come and talk to someone about it rather than just keep trying to push through.
How long have you been experiencing this difficulty with staying focused?

I’d say it’s been really noticeable for about… eleven months or so. It didn’t feel like it suddenly appeared overnight, exactly, but around that time the school changed the curriculum calendar, and we also started having these extra after-school planning meetings.

Since then, it’s like the amount of reading, planning, and keeping track of documents increased, or at least it started feeling much harder to keep up with. Before that I could usually push through, even if it took effort, but over the past eleven months it’s been much more obvious to me that I’m losing focus and having to reread things over and over.
Have you been feeling anxious, sad, or overwhelmed during this period of difficulty with focusing?

I’m not completely sure how to separate those things, to be honest. I wouldn’t say I’ve been walking around feeling sad all the time, or like there’s one big obvious emotional thing causing it. But I do feel… I suppose overwhelmed is probably the closest word, at least sometimes, because when I notice I’m behind or I’ve read the same thing three times and still haven’t absorbed it, I get frustrated with myself.

And then there’s a bit of anxiety that comes from the consequences of it, if that makes sense — like worrying I won’t finish marking in time, or that I’ll miss something important in a planning document. But I don’t know if I’d say the anxiety came first. It feels more like I start off trying to focus, then I lose the thread, then I get stressed because I’ve lost time. So… yes, overwhelmed at points, but I’m not sure it explains the focusing problem on its own.
Are you noticing any difficulties with focus or feeling overwhelmed in areas of your life outside of your teaching job?

Yes, unfortunately it’s not just school. Work is where it’s most obvious, because there are other people seeing the consequences, but at home it’s started showing up more than I’d like to admit.

Like, with work, the missed follow-through has got serious enough that my department chair has put me on a support plan. That was… honestly pretty embarrassing. It wasn’t one dramatic mistake, more like a pattern of me saying I’d finish something, or read something, or follow up on a piece of planning, and then either doing it late or realizing I’d completely lost track of it. So now there’s this formal structure around me, which I understand, but it feels awful.

And at home, my wife has started taking over things like bills and reminders because she says she can’t really count on me to keep track of them reliably. Not in a cruel way — she’s trying to keep everything from falling through the cracks — but it makes me feel quite useless. I’ll have every intention of remembering something or sorting it out, and then it just doesn’t happen unless she’s chasing it or doing it herself. So yes, it’s definitely outside of teaching too, just maybe less visible until it affects her directly.
Do you find that you're forgetting things more often than you used to, outside of just losing track of what you're reading or doing?

Yes, I think so. It’s not only that I lose the thread when I’m reading something — it’s more ordinary day-to-day responsibilities as well, which is a bit embarrassing to admit.

For example, I’ll see a parent email and think, “Right, I need to reply to that properly,” and then I’ll put it aside because I want to answer carefully, and suddenly it’s two days later and I haven’t done it. Or with bills, I’ll know something needs paying, and I’ll even think about doing it, but then the late notice comes before I’ve actually sorted it. And my wife might ask me to pick something up on the way home — something simple — and I’ll genuinely intend to do it, but unless I write it down immediately or she reminds me, I can get home and realize I completely forgot.

It’s those kinds of things. Not huge dramatic memory gaps, just… normal responsibilities slipping more often than they used to, and more often than I’m comfortable with.
Are you experiencing any low mood or depression?

I don’t think I’d call it depression, no. I mean, I do get fed up with myself, and there are days where I feel quite flat after something has gone wrong or I’ve realized I’ve let something slip again. But it feels more tied to those situations, if that makes sense, rather than waking up every day feeling hopeless or sad for no clear reason.

I’m not saying I’m cheerful about it all — I’m really not. It’s been wearing me down, especially feeling like I’m not managing things I should be able to manage. But “depressed” feels like a stronger word than what I’m experiencing. It’s more frustration, embarrassment, and feeling overwhelmed when things pile up.
Have you experienced any particularly stressful or traumatic events in the last year, aside from the changes at work?

No, I don’t think so. Not in the sense of a trauma or a major life event, anyway.

I mean, the work situation has obviously been stressful, and it’s sort of bled into everything else, but aside from that I can’t point to something like a bereavement, accident, or anything frightening that happened. Nothing like that. It’s more been this gradual build-up of ordinary things feeling harder to keep on top of, rather than one big event that set it off.

I suppose I hesitate because “stressful” can cover a lot, can’t it? There have been normal stresses — family stuff, money admin, the usual pressures — but nothing that stands out as a particular event in the last year. So no, not really.
Do you ever notice any physical sensations, like a racing heart or tightness in your chest, when you're feeling overwhelmed or anxious?

Not really, no — at least not in a way that I’ve clearly noticed. I don’t think I get the sort of racing heart or chest tightness you’re describing. When I’m overwhelmed, it’s more that I feel mentally overloaded, like there are too many things competing for my attention, rather than something very physical happening in my body.

I suppose there may be times when I’m tense without really registering it, but I wouldn’t say I’ve had episodes where I thought, “My heart’s pounding,” or “My chest feels tight.” If it has happened, it hasn’t been prominent enough for me to remember it as a pattern.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep over the past eleven months?

I’m not completely sure, to be honest. I haven’t really tracked it in any proper way, so it’s hard to say whether there’s been a clear change over the last eleven months specifically.

I mean, there have probably been nights where I’ve gone to bed later than I meant to, or where I’ve been lying there thinking about things I still need to do, but I don’t know if that’s new or just something I notice more when life feels a bit more pressured. I wouldn’t want to overstate it and say, “Yes, my sleep has dramatically changed,” because I don’t think that’s quite right.

So… I suppose the honest answer is I haven’t noticed a clear pattern. It might be a bit inconsistent at times, but I couldn’t point to a definite change in my sleep and say that started eleven months ago.
Have you noticed a decrease in your motivation to do things you normally enjoy?

I’m not sure I’d say a decrease in motivation exactly. It’s a bit hard to separate out, because with things I normally enjoy, I don’t think I’ve stopped wanting to do them in the sense of not caring about them anymore.

It’s more that sometimes getting started feels like more of a hurdle than it should, if that makes sense. Like I might think, “Oh, I’d like to watch that programme,” or “I should message someone back,” or “It would be nice to do something at the weekend,” but then the thought sits there and I don’t necessarily act on it straight away. But I’m not sure that’s the same as losing motivation or enjoyment.

When I actually do end up doing something I like, I can still enjoy it. So I wouldn’t say there’s been a clear loss of interest in things. I haven’t noticed a big change where I suddenly don’t want to do anything I used to like. It’s more… I don’t know, a bit patchy or inconsistent, maybe. But not a definite decrease in motivation, no.
Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with friends or family members due to your difficulties with focusing and following through on tasks?

Yes… unfortunately, yes. I think that’s probably one of the areas where it’s become harder to brush off as just me being a bit disorganised.

With friends and family, it’s not that I’ve fallen out with people exactly, but it has definitely put strain on things. At home especially, my wife has started taking over more of the bills and reminders and general keeping-track-of-life things, because she doesn’t really trust that I’ll remember or follow through consistently. And I don’t blame her, because there have been enough times where I’ve said, “Yes, I’ll sort that,” and then it just hasn’t happened, or I’ve remembered too late, or I’ve needed several reminders. But it still feels horrible, because it puts her in this position of having to manage me a bit, which isn’t fair.

At work it’s been more formal, I suppose. I’m a secondary school teacher, and the missed follow-through has got serious enough that my department chair has put me on a support plan. That was quite embarrassing, honestly. It wasn’t one single dramatic thing, more a pattern of things not being completed when I said they would be, or needing chasing, and eventually it became something they had to address properly.

So yes, I’d say it has affected relationships — particularly with my wife, and professionally with colleagues as well. It’s not that people have stopped caring about me, but I can tell they’re more cautious about relying on me, and that’s difficult.
Have you noticed any difficulties with decision-making or problem-solving?

I’m not sure, actually. I don’t think I’ve noticed a very clear problem-solving issue in the sense of, you know, being unable to work things out or not understanding what needs to happen.

Decision-making… maybe sometimes, but I’m not sure I’d want to describe it as a major thing. I can be a bit slow to decide if there are lots of small options, or if it feels like I need to pick the “right” way to do something. I might go back and forth in my head for longer than is really necessary. But I don’t know if that’s a separate difficulty or just me overcomplicating things a bit.

With practical problems, once I’m actually focused on them, I think I can usually solve them reasonably well. It’s more that I might take a while to settle on where to start, or I might leave a decision sitting there because I’m not quite ready to commit to it. But I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed some dramatic change where I suddenly can’t make decisions or solve problems.

So… yes and no, I suppose. There might be some hesitation or getting stuck on the starting point, but I haven’t really identified it as a distinct problem on its own.
Have you noticed any significant decline in your ability to learn new information?

No, I don’t think so. Not in any obvious or significant way, anyway.

I mean, I still feel like I can learn new information when I need to. If someone explains something to me properly, or if I sit down and actually engage with it, I can understand it and take it in. I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed that my memory or ability to learn has suddenly got worse, or that I’m unable to grasp new things.

Sometimes I might need to go over something more than once, but I think that’s fairly normal depending on how much is going on or how interested I am in the material. I haven’t had a sense of, “Oh, I used to be able to learn things and now I can’t.” It’s more that some information sticks better than other information, especially if it feels immediately relevant or I’ve properly focused on it.

So overall, no — I haven’t noticed a significant decline in learning new information.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms, such as headaches or fatigue, when you're struggling to focus or follow through on tasks?

I don’t think I’ve noticed anything very specific physically, no. Not in the sense that, when I can’t focus, I reliably get a headache or something like that.

I mean, I do sometimes feel worn out after I’ve spent ages trying to force myself through a task, but I’m not sure whether I’d call that a symptom exactly, or just the normal frustration and effort of sitting there pushing against something that isn’t happening. It’s more mental tiredness than anything I can point to physically. I wouldn’t say, “Oh yes, every time I struggle to follow through, I get headaches,” because that doesn’t really ring true.

With fatigue, I suppose it depends what you mean. I can feel drained by the process, especially if I’ve been trying to concentrate for a long time and not getting anywhere, but I haven’t noticed a clear physical pattern that I’d be confident describing. No major headaches or bodily symptoms that stand out to me.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite over the past eleven months?

Not really, no. I haven’t noticed any clear change in my appetite over that sort of period.

I mean, I haven’t been tracking it very carefully, so I suppose it’s possible there are day-to-day variations, like some days I’m hungrier than others or I eat later because I’m busy, but nothing that stands out as unusual or sustained. I wouldn’t say I’ve lost my appetite, and I wouldn’t say I’ve suddenly been eating a lot more either.

Over the past eleven months, I don’t think there’s been a pattern where I’d look back and think, “Yes, that changed.” My eating feels broadly the same as it usually is, as far as I can tell.
Do you find it hard to sustain your attention on tasks that require continuous mental effort?

Yes, definitely. That’s probably one of the main reasons I came in, honestly.

Like, I can sit down with a stack of essays to mark, or a curriculum document I need to read through, and I genuinely intend to do it. It’s not that I’m avoiding it on purpose or that I don’t understand the work. I’ll have everything in front of me, maybe even a pen in my hand, and I’ll think, “Right, I’m going to get through this properly now.”

And then ten minutes later I’ll realize I’ve been staring at the same page, or the same paragraph, and I’m not really taking it in. My eyes have been moving over the words, but my mind’s been somewhere else entirely — thinking about three different unrelated things, or what I need to do later, or just sort of drifting. Then I have to go back and reread the same bit again because I can’t honestly say I absorbed it.

It’s especially hard when the task needs steady mental effort and there isn’t something immediately engaging about it. Marking essays, reading policy documents, planning from a long document — those kinds of things can feel like I’m constantly having to drag my attention back to the page. I can start with good intentions, but sustaining it is the hard part.
When you find your mind drifting off, are you usually thinking about worries or concerns, or is it more that your mind is simply wandering without a specific focus?

It’s usually not one specific worry, no. I mean, sometimes I might drift onto something I need to do later, but it’s not like I’m sitting there consumed by one big concern or ruminating on a particular problem.

It’s more like my mind just… slips off the task. I’ll sit down with essays to mark or a curriculum document, fully intending to work through it properly, and then quite quickly — sometimes within ten minutes — I’ll realize I’ve been looking at the same page without really absorbing it. And when I notice what I’ve been thinking about, it’s usually three unrelated things at once, or half-thoughts, or just general wandering.

So it’s less, “I’m too worried to concentrate,” and more, “I’m physically here, the work is in front of me, but my attention has wandered off somewhere else and I haven’t taken in what I’ve just read.” Then I have to pull myself back and reread it, which gets frustrating because I did sit down genuinely meaning to do it.
Do you often find yourself avoiding tasks or activities because they require a lot of mental effort or attention?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that, because I don’t know if I’d call it “avoiding” in a deliberate way.

I don’t usually think, “I refuse to do that because it takes concentration.” It’s more that if something looks like it’s going to need a lot of sustained focus, I can feel myself putting it off or circling around it. I’ll do smaller, easier bits first, or I’ll convince myself I just need to get set up properly before starting, and then quite a lot of time can pass before I actually begin.

But I’m not sure how often that counts as avoidance versus just… struggling to get into it. With work things, I still know they need doing, so I do eventually try to tackle them. It’s just that tasks requiring a lot of mental effort can feel like a big hurdle, and I may delay them longer than I mean to.
Did you have significant difficulties with focus, organization, or follow-through on tasks as a child?

Yes, I think so. Looking back, it was there pretty early, even in primary school.

I remember my report cards having comments like, “bright but careless,” which came up more than once, and things along the lines of, “doesn’t finish work unless closely supervised.” At the time I think everyone just took it as me being a bit messy or not trying hard enough, because I could understand the work when I was actually doing it. But I’d lose track of what I was meant to be doing, or I’d start something and not quite get it finished unless the teacher was really on top of me.

And my parents were always finding worksheets crumpled up in my backpack — like, completed or half-completed sheets that I’d just forgotten to hand in. They’d ask, “Why is this still in your bag?” and I honestly wouldn’t have a good answer. I hadn’t decided not to turn it in; it had just sort of disappeared from my mind once it went into the bag.

So yes, I’d say the focus and follow-through side of things was definitely an issue when I was a child, even if nobody framed it that way at the time.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or suspected to have Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in the past?

Not formally, no — at least, not that I know of.

I don’t remember anyone ever saying, “This is what you have,” or being assessed for it properly when I was younger. I think the difficulties were noticed in a more informal way — teachers commenting that I was careless or disorganised, my parents getting frustrated with me — but it was never really framed as a possible diagnosis.

As an adult, I suppose I’ve wondered about it more recently, partly because I’ve started to notice patterns rather than just individual failures, if that makes sense. But I haven’t previously had a diagnosis, and I haven’t gone through a formal assessment before this.

It’s more that sometimes getting started feels like more of a hurdle than it should, if that makes sense. Like I might think, “Oh, I’d like to watch that programme,” or “I should message someone back,” or “It would be nice to do something at the weekend,” but then the thought sits there and I don’t necessarily act on it straight away. But I’m not sure that’s the same as losing motivation or enjoyment.

When I actually do end up doing something I like, I can still enjoy it. So I wouldn’t say there’s been a clear loss of interest in things. I haven’t noticed a big change where I suddenly don’t want to do anything I used to like. It’s more… I don’t know, a bit patchy or inconsistent, maybe. But not a definite decrease in motivation, no.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting social relationships
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with friends or family members due to your difficulties with focusing and following through on tasks?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work, the missed follow-through has become serious enough that my department chair put me on a support plan, and at home my wife has started taking over bills and reminders because she can’t count on me to keep track of them.
target_item.reason: The question asks about the impact of focusing and follow-through difficulties on relationships with family or friends, which is most directly about functional impairment, especially the strain at home where my wife has had to take over bills and reminders.

patient.answer:
Yes… unfortunately, yes. I think that’s probably one of the areas where it’s become harder to brush off as just me being a bit disorganised.

With friends and family, it’s not that I’ve fallen out with people exactly, but it has definitely put strain on things. At home especially, my wife has started taking over more of the bills and reminders and general keeping-track-of-life things, because she doesn’t really trust that I’ll remember or follow through consistently. And I don’t blame her, because there have been enough times where I’ve said, “Yes, I’ll sort that,” and then it just hasn’t happened, or I’ve remembered too late, or I’ve needed several reminders. But it still feels horrible, because it puts her in this position of having to manage me a bit, which isn’t fair.

At work it’s been more formal, I suppose. I’m a secondary school teacher, and the missed follow-through has got serious enough that my department chair has put me on a support plan. That was quite embarrassing, honestly. It wasn’t one single dramatic thing, more a pattern of things not being completed when I said they would be, or needing chasing, and eventually it became something they had to address properly.

So yes, I’d say it has affected relationships — particularly with my wife, and professionally with colleagues as well. It’s not that people have stopped caring about me, but I can tell they’re more cautious about relying on me, and that’s difficult.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any cognitive difficulties beyond attention and memory
doctor.question: Have you noticed any difficulties with decision-making or problem-solving?

target_item.reason: The question asks specifically about decision-making or problem-solving, which is not directly covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure, actually. I don’t think I’ve noticed a very clear problem-solving issue in the sense of, you know, being unable to work things out or not understanding what needs to happen.

Decision-making… maybe sometimes, but I’m not sure I’d want to describe it as a major thing. I can be a bit slow to decide if there are lots of small options, or if it feels like I need to pick the “right” way to do something. I might go back and forth in my head for longer than is really necessary. But I don’t know if that’s a separate difficulty or just me overcomplicating things a bit.

With practical problems, once I’m actually focused on them, I think I can usually solve them reasonably well. It’s more that I might take a while to settle on where to start, or I might leave a decision sitting there because I’m not quite ready to commit to it. But I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed some dramatic change where I suddenly can’t make decisions or solve problems.

So… yes and no, I suppose. There might be some hesitation or getting stuck on the starting point, but I haven’t really identified it as a distinct problem on its own.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any significant cognitive decline
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant decline in your ability to learn new information?

target_item.reason: The question is about a significant decline in ability to learn new information, which is not specifically covered by the listed ADHD inattentive symptom profile; the profile describes attention, follow-through, losing items, forgetfulness, onset, impairment, and duration rather than a decline in learning capacity.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so. Not in any obvious or significant way, anyway.

I mean, I still feel like I can learn new information when I need to. If someone explains something to me properly, or if I sit down and actually engage with it, I can understand it and take it in. I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed that my memory or ability to learn has suddenly got worse, or that I’m unable to grasp new things.

Sometimes I might need to go over something more than once, but I think that’s fairly normal depending on how much is going on or how interested I am in the material. I haven’t had a sense of, “Oh, I used to be able to learn things and now I can’t.” It’s more that some information sticks better than other information, especially if it feels immediately relevant or I’ve properly focused on it.

So overall, no — I haven’t noticed a significant decline in learning new information.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any physical symptoms related to their difficulties
doctor.question: Have you noticed any physical symptoms, such as headaches or fatigue, when you're struggling to focus or follow through on tasks?

target_item.reason: The question asks about physical symptoms such as headaches or fatigue, which are not covered by the provided ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think I’ve noticed anything very specific physically, no. Not in the sense that, when I can’t focus, I reliably get a headache or something like that.

I mean, I do sometimes feel worn out after I’ve spent ages trying to force myself through a task, but I’m not sure whether I’d call that a symptom exactly, or just the normal frustration and effort of sitting there pushing against something that isn’t happening. It’s more mental tiredness than anything I can point to physically. I wouldn’t say, “Oh yes, every time I struggle to follow through, I get headaches,” because that doesn’t really ring true.

With fatigue, I suppose it depends what you mean. I can feel drained by the process, especially if I’ve been trying to concentrate for a long time and not getting anywhere, but I haven’t noticed a clear physical pattern that I’d be confident describing. No major headaches or bodily symptoms that stand out to me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any significant changes in appetite
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your appetite over the past eleven months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about appetite changes, which are not covered by any of the provided ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Not really, no. I haven’t noticed any clear change in my appetite over that sort of period.

I mean, I haven’t been tracking it very carefully, so I suppose it’s possible there are day-to-day variations, like some days I’m hungrier than others or I eat later because I’m busy, but nothing that stands out as unusual or sustained. I wouldn’t say I’ve lost my appetite, and I wouldn’t say I’ve suddenly been eating a lot more either.

Over the past eleven months, I don’t think there’s been a pattern where I’d look back and think, “Yes, that changed.” My eating feels broadly the same as it usually is, as far as I can tell.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty with sustaining attention during tasks
doctor.question: Do you find it hard to sustain your attention on tasks that require continuous mental effort?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can sit down with a stack of essays or a curriculum document fully intending to work, and within ten minutes I realize I’ve been staring at the same page, thinking about three other things, and barely taking in what’s in front of me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about difficulty sustaining attention during tasks requiring continuous mental effort.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. That’s probably one of the main reasons I came in, honestly.

Like, I can sit down with a stack of essays to mark, or a curriculum document I need to read through, and I genuinely intend to do it. It’s not that I’m avoiding it on purpose or that I don’t understand the work. I’ll have everything in front of me, maybe even a pen in my hand, and I’ll think, “Right, I’m going to get through this properly now.”

And then ten minutes later I’ll realize I’ve been staring at the same page, or the same paragraph, and I’m not really taking it in. My eyes have been moving over the words, but my mind’s been somewhere else entirely — thinking about three different unrelated things, or what I need to do later, or just sort of drifting. Then I have to go back and reread the same bit again because I can’t honestly say I absorbed it.

It’s especially hard when the task needs steady mental effort and there isn’t something immediately engaging about it. Marking essays, reading policy documents, planning from a long document — those kinds of things can feel like I’m constantly having to drag my attention back to the page. I can start with good intentions, but sustaining it is the hard part.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences mind-wandering as a primary issue
doctor.question: When you find your mind drifting off, are you usually thinking about worries or concerns, or is it more that your mind is simply wandering without a specific focus?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can sit down with a stack of essays or a curriculum document fully intending to work, and within ten minutes I realize I’ve been staring at the same page, thinking about three other things, and barely taking in what’s in front of me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about what happens when attention drifts during tasks requiring sustained mental effort, which directly relates to difficulty sustaining attention.

patient.answer:
It’s usually not one specific worry, no. I mean, sometimes I might drift onto something I need to do later, but it’s not like I’m sitting there consumed by one big concern or ruminating on a particular problem.

It’s more like my mind just… slips off the task. I’ll sit down with essays to mark or a curriculum document, fully intending to work through it properly, and then quite quickly — sometimes within ten minutes — I’ll realize I’ve been looking at the same page without really absorbing it. And when I notice what I’ve been thinking about, it’s usually three unrelated things at once, or half-thoughts, or just general wandering.

So it’s less, “I’m too worried to concentrate,” and more, “I’m physically here, the work is in front of me, but my attention has wandered off somewhere else and I haven’t taken in what I’ve just read.” Then I have to pull myself back and reread it, which gets frustrating because I did sit down genuinely meaning to do it.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of avoidance behaviors
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself avoiding tasks or activities because they require a lot of mental effort or attention?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about avoiding tasks or activities because they require sustained mental effort, but the provided symptom profile does not include an avoidance/procrastination item. S002 covers difficulty sustaining attention once engaged, not avoidance of such tasks.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure how to answer that, because I don’t know if I’d call it “avoiding” in a deliberate way.

I don’t usually think, “I refuse to do that because it takes concentration.” It’s more that if something looks like it’s going to need a lot of sustained focus, I can feel myself putting it off or circling around it. I’ll do smaller, easier bits first, or I’ll convince myself I just need to get set up properly before starting, and then quite a lot of time can pass before I actually begin.

But I’m not sure how often that counts as avoidance versus just… struggling to get into it. With work things, I still know they need doing, so I do eventually try to tackle them. It’s just that tasks requiring a lot of mental effort can feel like a big hurdle, and I may delay them longer than I mean to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are better explained by a neurodevelopmental disorder
doctor.question: Did you have significant difficulties with focus, organization, or follow-through on tasks as a child?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in primary school, my report cards said things like “bright but careless” and “doesn’t finish work unless closely supervised,” and my parents were always finding worksheets crumpled in my backpack that I had forgotten to turn in.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether these attention/follow-through difficulties were present during childhood, which directly relates to onset before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think so. Looking back, it was there pretty early, even in primary school.

I remember my report cards having comments like, “bright but careless,” which came up more than once, and things along the lines of, “doesn’t finish work unless closely supervised.” At the time I think everyone just took it as me being a bit messy or not trying hard enough, because I could understand the work when I was actually doing it. But I’d lose track of what I was meant to be doing, or I’d start something and not quite get it finished unless the teacher was really on top of me.

And my parents were always finding worksheets crumpled up in my backpack — like, completed or half-completed sheets that I’d just forgotten to hand in. They’d ask, “Why is this still in your bag?” and I honestly wouldn’t have a good answer. I hadn’t decided not to turn it in; it had just sort of disappeared from my mind once it went into the bag.

So yes, I’d say the focus and follow-through side of things was definitely an issue when I was a child, even if nobody framed it that way at the time.

inference.note: R41.0 was ruled out as the patient's symptoms are more consistent with attentional difficulties rather than memory or cognitive decline

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are better explained by ADHD or another condition
doctor.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with or suspected to have Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in the past?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about prior ADHD diagnosis or suspicion, which is not covered by the listed symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Not formally, no — at least, not that I know of.

I don’t remember anyone ever saying, “This is what you have,” or being assessed for it properly when I was younger. I think the difficulties were noticed in a more informal way — teachers commenting that I was careless or disorganised, my parents getting frustrated with me — but it was never really framed as a possible diagnosis.

As an adult, I suppose I’ve wondered about it more recently, partly because I’ve started to notice patterns rather than just individual failures, if that makes sense. But I haven’t previously had a diagnosis, and I haven’t gone through a formal assessment before this.
